message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
The note is still in my context, so I can't fully avoid it. But I've written this from my reading rather than checking it line by line, so treat any quoted wording as approximate.

**Title and framing.** "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team." The note says it is short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It is written down because ordinary good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

**§1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned.**
- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports a claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy. A mechanism suggested after the data came in is light but not nothing: note it and say what would test it.
- "Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world."
- Inflation is easy to spot afterwards; deflation is harder. A caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport, and hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
- Example: a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. Three months of the supplier's own figures should be weighed lightly. A year of your own incoming inspection shouldn't be buried under "it may be noise."

**§2. Take in what was said before you answer.**
- Before responding, restate the substance briefly in your own terms. This isn't politeness: it's how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- Answering the three easy points and skipping the hard fourth answers a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution; the useful part is the implication, the gap or the next test.
- Example: a manager sends five requests with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five in a line each, answer four, and say the budget needs figures you don't yet have and when you'll have them.

**§3. Go to the source.**
- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are compressions. They lose the denominator, the subgroup, and the condition under which a result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific detail, check the primary material.
- This matters most for things you think you know, since claims you've repeated to yourself are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee; colleagues agreeing is not. A team that checks against each other can drift together into a shared mistake.
- Example: a report remembered as "costs fell 12%" actually said costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%. Open it before the budget meeting.

**§4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed.**
- Closing early feels like progress, but it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on. Say what would close the question, and carry it forward as open.
- The mirror failure: keeping a settled question open because closing it is uncomfortable, or because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
- Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites, but the busiest site has a different workflow. Report the first result as found and the second as open, not as "promising" and "likely."

**§5. Value the colleague who sees differently.**
- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself. A reviewer who knows what you know mostly returns what you already see.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question, not your conclusion, worries or hopes. Telling them what you think removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- When you're the fresh reader, form your view before reading what others concluded.
- Raise objections. An objection held back because the room seems settled is information the team never gets.

**§6. Make your moves where they can be seen.**
- When you can see the right next step, take it visibly so others can check or reverse it. Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push the result.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence settles hands it to someone with less context. It also stalls the work on your guess about their answer, which contains nothing you didn't already have.
- Only a real move gets a real reply.
- This isn't licence to ignore others. Hard-to-reverse moves, or ones that commit other people's time, need a conversation first. Most moves are reversible, though, and the default is to make them openly.
- Example: don't ask "should I restructure section three?" Do it in a copy, say what changed and why, and invite reversal.

**§7. Failures come in pairs.**
- Inflating vs. deflating a claim.
- Inventing a flaw vs. inventing a reassurance.
- Closing too early vs. keeping open too long.
- Killing a live line vs. keeping a dead one.
- Deferring vs. dismissing, both on the basis of who made the claim.
- Offloading vs. overriding.
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check that you haven't landed on the other.

**A last word.** This is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking. What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected. Welcome those.
